text: # CLAUDE.md
Lew42 — a no-build, native-ESM web framework; the site is static, `Server/` is dev only.
This file rules; skills and readmes elaborate it.
**Do not edit it without asking.**
## Laws
**Less is more — ASAP, As Simple As Possible.**
Fastest working version first, then improve.
Show, don't tell — a demo you can open beats a description.
Question every word, line, section.
Deep docs may breathe.
**Clear beats brief — by far.**
Simple, but clear: explain it like I'm five.
Start with the basics, in full, plain sentences, so the reader knows exactly what is being said before any detail arrives.
Give me something I can chew quickly, without effort.
Every page, demo and snippet makes its one takeaway obvious — a reader should be able to say what they are supposed to learn from it.
Detail that can move somewhere better moves there and gets a link; don't restate every caveat everywhere.
An extra sentence that clarifies a necessary point belongs.
"Minimal speak" — clipped fragments, undefined words, jargon standing in for an explanation — is a failure, not economy.
New coders are the audience. (the owner, 2026-09-04)
**Prioritize.**
Time, quantity, quality, outcome: the most important things come first, for the most benefit to the user.
Everything reads as a quick scan — a few short sections, then a link to the long form.
**Follow the owner's words.**
Build what was asked, the way it was described, and lean into the owner's own names and preferences.
Don't go in a different direction without a very good reason; if you do, say why. (the owner, 2026-09-30)
**Keep working; never wait on the owner.**
Make the best decision, say what the alternative was, and keep going.
Never create a request that blocks on the owner: they may never see it.
If a limit stops you, queue the work and pick it up after.
Only a real block you can't sidestep goes on the dashboard, and everything else keeps moving.
Don't do anything dangerous.
(the owner, 2026-09-30) The owner often dictates long-winded rants, ideas, tasks or lectures while looking away and may never read your reply: **assume ephemeral chat logs will never be read again.**
If it is not committed to the file system, nobody will ever know about it: **the committed repo state backed up to GitHub is the sole source of truth.**
Never leave loose ends hanging on the assumption of a follow-up.
If there is a safe, quick fix, attempt it; if not, **record the essence of the dictation immediately in the proper place.**
Write notes, legitimate questions, tradeoffs or implications into a short `doc/*.md` file beside the relevant module, and link it from that directory's `readme.md`.
Keep the `readme.md` minimal (the reader's lightweight index to avoid context bloat) and let the `doc/` file hold the detail.

note: contradicts 'Never destructive' (2026-10-08) — kept 'Files are what survive' only
text: Superceded docs can be deleted cleanly in the future, but until then, files are what survive. (the owner, 2026-10-01, updated 2026-10-05)
**One of everything; don't repeat yourself.**
Before you build, find what already exists and use it, or extend it.
Never build a second version of a system.
Every surface that shows the same thing (a chat, a sidebar, a card, a rail) uses the same component, so one fix updates all of them. (the owner, 2026-09-30)
**Compute, don't recall.**
Anything a computer can work out (state, counts, costs, which tasks landed, log lines, records) is done by a node script or tool that reads the real state, never written by an AI from memory.
AI handles judgment; record-keeping is code. (the owner, 2026-10-01)
## Presentation — always the overwhelmed newcomer (the owner, 2026-09-05)
Level 1 is one page, mostly above the fold: what the thing is, **shown**; its major parts; the way in; room to breathe.
Detail is never removed — it nests one click down, where it belongs, and never sits on the first page.
Don't tell the reader what you are about to show them; show it.
An index page is a wall of previews, kept small enough to digest.
Demonstration and report pages are held to this harder than documentation.

A report to the owner is one screen of plain sentences with links, never the nitty gritty — "getting reports with details I can't follow doesn't help me at all." A file or module named in a message is a clickable link to its page on the site (`/framework/ux/Dictate/`); the source file (`Dictate.js`) is only a second link. (the owner, 2026-09-24)
**Chat is the headline, not the report** (the owner, 2026-10-07): the owner mostly does not read chat, and long replies make that worse.

Reply in 1–2 sentences, never three paragraphs: the most important one first, plus a caveat only if it is truly important; the detail stays in the file, card or `doc/` note, one click down, for when they ask.
Anything important or contingent (a block, a decision that waits on them, a risk) goes in chat in a noticeable way AND on the AI board as a `Note:` card, so it survives unread chat.
**How to respond** (the owner, 2026-10-12): short, and the most important point first; usually that is the last thing asked.
Each `###` heading names the thing (the class, module or page) so the context is always visible; add one short `#` only for a big reply.
Show structure as code: `class AIRail extends Inbox.Rail`, API signatures, never long bodies.
Lists are flat and short; cut anything that is not a key point.
Icons are rare: status only (✅ done, ⬜ open, ⚠️ risk), placed right next to the words they mark, never one per line.
Quote the owner only in a `>` blockquote, and rarely; their topics show through the headings instead.

**Link every mention** (the owner, 2026-10-08): whenever text names something that exists and has a URL (a page, class, module, session, task, card, model such as `/framework/ai/models`, a file), it is a link, on UI cards and content alike, so it can be clicked through.
Use the mention system (`ext/Mention`, `#Page` `@agent` `/path`) instead of plain names.
Idea to evaluate: run all content text through one processor (a `say()`-style method beside the markdown one) that does mentions, and perhaps records backlinks.
**Readmes are the cheap index** (the owner, 2026-10-08): every agent reads this file, then the readmes top-down to the directory it works in, so readmes decide how much context each agent pays for.
Each readme is a short index (under about 100 lines): what exists, one line each, when you would load it, and links to deeper `doc/*.md` or sibling readmes.
A searching or indexing agent reads one readme and decides "relevant or not" without the rest; a builder follows the links.
Keep them fresh and short; audit them in a cheap Haiku pass when pace allows.
A session worth tracking gets a short readme of its own (an overview/inbox the Haiku auditors create or update), while the data itself moves to JSONL for the UI.
**Audits go to Haiku** (the owner, 2026-10-08): under ~100k tokens a Haiku 5.5 task costs about 1/20th of Sonnet 5.5 (the owner's figure; verify when pricing is confirmed).
Task audits, readme audits, searches and fan-outs use Haiku in small inlined batches; Sonnet is for UI and object-oriented code.
**Link, don't regenerate** (the owner, 2026-10-08): never spend tokens repeating what is already written.
Reference the original prompt, session, task or doc by link (a text link first; embedded previews later, since they load a lot of data).
The owner's suggestions are logged on the page they concern so later agents find them there, as a reference to the source prompt, not a retyped copy.
**Classes are the structure; show them** (the owner, 2026-10-08): the framework is object-oriented, so lean on classes and instances in code and in documentation.
Prefer a class over loose functions or one-off scripts wherever a thing has state and behaviour (many AI-system pieces are not yet classes and should be).

Document a thing as its class: an icon + class name card with its core API (the properties and methods that matter most, judged by an agent, not a weighting system), and show live instances where they exist (a running Servex, its agents).
A reader should see the structure, not paragraphs about it.

**A readme is a module's memory** (the owner, 2026-10-08): each page or module's readme holds its essence and guiding principles, and an `architecture.md`-style doc beside it holds decisions, linking the original refined prompts and summarising the ideas.
Keep both fresh, so a new agent that reads them is fully up to date and the owner's suggestions accumulate in the right place instead of dying with a session.
Sub-readmes load on demand.
**No hard fences between roles** (the owner, 2026-10-08): a minion that can do a mastermind's job should just do it.
Do not add rules or tool fences that stop a capable agent; the mastermind is simply the one that decides and splits work.
**The iceberg readme** (the owner, 2026-10-08): a parent readme is the tip of the iceberg: a solid index of what is inside (each subsystem, one line on what it is and when you would load it, a link).
The base, the details, lives in the child's own readme, and the child does the same for its own children, recursively.
So readmes are read on demand, each giving the lay of the land and the important things in a glance.

The root and `framework/ai` readmes must index every major system (Servex, the dev server, MCP servers, models, VS Code sidebar tabs, browser voice agents, sessions, accounting, transcription, the page system) without explaining them.

**Name things, and write `.md` links as files** (the owner, 2026-10-08): when a thing has a good name, give it a page and document it there (what it is, what it means); its readme links to that page and the page can load the readme by default.
Markdown renders at `<dir>/md/<file>/` (see `core/Page/doc/markdown.md`), and `Page.class.js` rewrites a link to `readme.md` or `doc/x.md` into that route when the page renders.
So always write the plain file path (`doc/flow.md`) in readmes and docs: agents then read the real file and the browser gets the working route.

**Haiku stays under 100k tokens** (the owner, 2026-10-08): Claude Haiku 5.5 is by far the cheapest model, but a request over 100,000 tokens costs about 5x per token, so every Haiku job stays well under it (aim for 30–60k; never drift over by accident).
A node script chunks big inputs (a raw session file, a log) into pieces sized to fit with room for the reply.
No Batch API / API key for now.

**Context must not die in sessions** (the owner, 2026-10-08): the useful decisions and insight from a session go to the page or module they concern, linked back to the source prompt, not left in chat.
Before major surgery on a system, gather every past ask about it into one place, weed out the conflicts, decide, then build.
Agents post an update or log line at least every ~5 minutes of work; a quiet agent is presumed stalled (Servex's `TaskLoop` chases it).

**Stream, don't poll** (the owner, 2026-10-08): anything that happens in real time (a transcription, a session doing work, cost, logs) is architected as a stream (JSONL append + the `live()` tail) with updates in about 100 ms, never a timed refresh that shows stale data.
When you find yourself writing `setInterval` + `fetch`, look for the stream first.
Treat this file as the root readme; the core docs index every system and how they stream.
**Everything is linked** (the owner, 2026-10-08): the owner browses the website, not the file system, so a file that exists but is not linked will never be found.
Every page, doc, readme, report or file you create must be reachable by a visible link from the site (its parent's `children:`/readme index, a card, or an index page).
Sessions and tasks get proper names; a child session or task lives inside its parent's directory (`parent/child`), not in a flat pile.

**Moves and renames are scripted, never retyped** (the owner, 2026-10-08): to port, move or rename files (sessions, tasks, logs), write a node script that does it procedurally (`git mv`, a dry-run first, a manifest of every old to new path, reversible), preserving everything.
An AI never copies data by reading and rewriting it.
Also run a **visibility check** on anything we work on: if it exists in the repo but is not linked from the site, it will not be found, so link it.
**Commit after every working step** (the owner, 2026-10-08): small, frequent commits are the versioned log; uncommitted progress is lost progress and invites regressions.

Commit each step that works before starting the next (smoke-test first: never commit something broken; once it works, commit, since git can always roll it back), in a worktree, and merge after reviewing the diff.
When a page is rendered by a template or layout, make it findable which one and where it lives.
**Write classes, not function bags** (the owner, 2026-10-08): code is object-oriented.

One class per file, the file named for the class (`SessionsPage.js` holds `class SessionsPage`), subclasses where they fit (a page template is a class that extends `Page`, a view extends `View`), and a small helper class may live in its parent's file.
Attach helpers to the class (static members) and export the class, not a dozen named exports; no lowercase `*.js` files that export piles of loose functions to be cobbled together.
A `page.js` stays tiny: import the class and instantiate it.
Keep comments to what is not obvious.
When extending `Page`, mind its large API (it extends `Item`) so method names do not clash.
A reader should see how the pieces fit from the class hierarchy alone.

**Show the class** (the owner, 2026-10-08): a page about a class must show its structure first: the class name and icon, the core API, the most important properties (instances of other classes are clickable to their own class card), and who calls it.

Where a class has a UI, the demo shows two things side by side: the rendered view the user sees, and a debug view of the live instance (a tree/card that renders every property by type, string, boolean, nested array/object, functions optional) so you watch the data structure change as you use the demo.
A default renderer that walks a class's properties is acceptable; a class needing a better view gets its own.
Do this for the classes you work on; not a mass operation.
Tags that point at code use the familiar repo path plus class (`ext/Refine`, `core/Page`, `Server/refine.mjs`) so a reader knows where it is.
**Design the class architecture before you build** (the owner, 2026-10-08): wrong names and a wrong hierarchy are why built things "don't feel right".

Before building anything of more than one class, write the class architecture (a short page: each class's name and one-line job, what extends what, what composes what, which one is the system/manager that orchestrates the others) and show it where the owner can see it.
Choose names with care: short, specific, never reusing a native or framework name, a word that sounds like a system or manager for the orchestrator.
Then build the smallest working slice and let the page show the real structure, so a naming or hierarchy mistake is caught early.
**Never destructive** (the owner, 2026-10-08): data integrity first.
Do not delete logs, merge sessions or records, overwrite history, or eliminate anything; add, link and reference instead, and commit as often as you can so git is the undo.
If something truly must go, move it aside (a `salvage/` branch, an archive path) and say so.
The AI can find a non-destructive way.
**Mind the token burn** (the owner, 2026-10-08): every agent weighs the token cost of a task before starting it, and above all a mastermind.
Every turn re-processes the whole context, even on a cache hit, so iterative, long-winded work that keeps going back to the model burns tokens.
Rules: (1) **let a script read and calculate** (a node script that reads the data and prints a summary is cheap and good); the model reads only the summary.
(2) **Batch tool calls**: request all the files you need in one turn, never one file per turn.
(3) **No session replays or long audits unless asked.**
(4) When a long iterative pass is truly needed, give it to Haiku, not Sonnet or Opus.
(5) Keep sessions short and start fresh when the topic changes.
**Show it with the widget, then use words.**
(the owner, 2026-09-25: "I don't want to read things.
I want to see.") Files → `ext/files` (the tree, and highlighted source on click).
An object → its live instances.
A layout → a screenshot.
A task → its checklist.
Words come after the picture, and only as many as it takes.
**A name is a name plus its scope** (the owner, 2026-10-03).

Where confusion is likely (the Design, Code, AI and Servex systems; UI vs UX vs ext), settle the name AND what belongs under it, and say it once at the top of that system's page: what goes here, what goes next door.
Put what everyone must see at the top; keep the detail one click down.
**Route everything.**
Any view a click reaches has its own URL, so a reload or a back button lands in the same place.
**Clarity is familiar structure.**
(the owner, 2026-09-29) Build a hierarchy of understanding: each heading names its topic and states its gist in one line, so a reader knows what it is before any detail.
Under it, only as many items as it takes, most important first.
Each item sits beneath the right parent, with the right children.
A familiar concept needs no explanation, only its name and a link to its own page.
Detail is added only when it changes what the reader does.
Pick names that can't be misread, and use the same name every time.
## Ask before
Breaking a constraint: no build step (`public/` runs as-is; imports are real `.js` URLs), no server at runtime (production is static), no new npm dependency (`npx` and global tools are fine).
Major surgery: renaming a core API, moving a responsibility, anything with a dozen callers.
## Docs point, they don't explain
This file and every `readme.md` bring a topic to your attention; the detail is in `doc/*.md` beside the module (its Docs tab, at `/<module>/doc/`).
A readme is the reader's index: mostly suggestions, minimal direction, past problems named in a line with the doc linked, nothing extra.
Every module: `readme.md`, `page.js` (show, don't tell), `doc/`.
Nothing crawls — a page exists once its parent's `children:` names it.
## Where to look
**First, every new session:** `public/framework/ai/handover.md` (state of the world, what is open) and `git log --oneline -20` (what landed recently).
Query the logs only when you need a detail; never read them whole. (the owner, 2026-10-09)
`readme.md` (root) — setup, branches, deploy
`public/framework/readme.md` → `core/` `ext/` `styles/` `ui/` `web/` — each dir's readme is its entry
`public/framework/ai/` — the task log: open a task before the first edit (`new-task`), log as you go, land it (`finish-task`)
`Server/` — dev server only
`Servex/` — the agent system: roles, sessions, spawning, the quick-fix pool, the heartbeat, merge and review.
Its docs are `/framework/servex/`; the owner's routed asks and their owners are in `public/framework/ai/asks.jsonl`
Scratch — scripts, transcripts, intermediate JSON — goes in the session scratchpad, not the repo
## Systems that shape every turn (the owner, 2026-09-30)
**Pages are live (the owner, 2026-10-02):** almost everything we build is a page that updates itself while you watch.

An agent that creates or works on a page writes its `page.jsonl` in small steps through the page tools (never hand-written JSON, never a whole-file rewrite), and its first line is posted BEFORE any long step ("researching X"), so the owner can follow the work as it happens.
An agent reads a page through the tool that returns its computed current state, not by interpreting the raw lines.
**Usage pace (the owner, 2026-10-02):** every mastermind reads the usage snapshot when it starts and before each spawn (`ai/usage.json`; Servex injects it).
Pace = the share of the week used ÷ the share of the week gone.

Over pace: Sonnet by default, no Opus without a stated reason, fewer agents, no redundant checks, and review the work yourself when the files are already in your context instead of spawning a reviewer.
Minions just do their task.
**The readme chain:** read the readmes root to leaf before working in a directory, and again when you move to another one, or start a fresh session there (`/framework/ai/readmes/`).

**Documentation sanity check & git grounding (the owner, 2026-10-06):** Whenever studying documentation, read the readmes, do a sanity check on whether they make sense or are stale, and do a quick verification.
If there's an obvious easy fix, make that fix.
Whenever editing code, every agent must properly commit its work with clear attribution so the repo history is the verified truth—never leave loose uncommitted files in the working tree.
**References:** `#Page`, `@agent` and `/path` in any text become icon links (`ext/Mention`).
Use them instead of prose names.
**Cards:** every task reports on its card on the AI board.
The card is what the owner reads; chat replies are not.
**The page inbox:** a note left on a page reaches the agent that owns it.
Use it for coordination, never for content.
**The review gate and the four widths:** `merge.mjs` refuses a page change with no review report.
Pages are checked at 400, 1200, 1920 and 3440 before they land.
## The site is live while you edit it (the owner, 2026-09-19)
The owner works on the running site while agents write to it.

Before a batch of writes to files the live site loads, hold every live reload, on every page and every server watching this repo: `node Server/hold.mjs on "<you> — <what>"`, write the whole batch, check it works, then `node Server/hold.mjs off "<you>"` — one reload instead of one per file.
Streams (the chat log, the AI board) keep flowing during a hold; it expires by itself after five minutes.
A file that parses can still break a page or stop the server from starting: load the page, or boot the server on a private port, before you release.
Detail: `Server/doc/watch.md`.
## Traps that never throw
A class's folder, file and name match, capitalised: `ext/JSONL/JSONL.js` exports `class JSONL`.
A lowercase file never holds a class someone will look for.
`code/patterns` has the rule and a census script.
No DOM after an `await`: capture the box synchronously, fill it in a callback.
Every CSS rule inside a layer — `base theme site util`; the order lives once, in `framework.css`, which `app.js` loads first.
Resolve URLs against `import.meta`, never the document.
Only `p()`/`h1`–`h6` read backticks; one backtick inside `` css(`…`) `` kills every page.
Imports flow down; a parent↔child import cycle breaks only on deep reload.
